timingRules.reason: HSE (Ireland) suggests avoiding tummy time just after a feed, especially if your baby has reflux. HSE gives no number of minutes; keeping about 30 minutes clear is Trunk’s planning convention.
HSE (Ireland) suggests avoiding tummy time just before a feed, especially if your baby has reflux. HSE gives no number of minutes; the 15 minutes is Trunk’s planning convention.
Quiet, familiar activities can fit the time before a nap. This is Trunk’s planning preference, not a sleep rule: no activity guarantees sleep, and the 30 minutes is a convention.

timingRules.cue: Better earlier, not right before a nap
timingRules.reason: Active, loud, or messy play fits earlier in the window, leaving calmer time and tidy-up before a planned nap. A planning preference, not a rule.
Children often wake slowly, so Trunk prefers something gentle first. There’s no required waiting time; follow your child.
Trunk puts something gentle first after a nap and saves lively play for a little later. A preference, not a waiting rule.

activities.title: Chest-to-chest tummy time
activities.summary: Recline, awake and supported, with your baby tummy-down on your chest, and chat face to face.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

supervision.space: Reclined in a chair, on a bed, or on the floor with your head supported—only while you're wide awake.

steps: Recline with your head and back supported so you can see your baby's face.
Lay your baby tummy-down on your chest, one hand resting on their back.
Talk, smile, and make big expressions so they lift their head to look at you.
As they get stronger over the weeks, recline a little flatter.
adaptations: Very new baby: a minute or two is plenty; let them rest their cheek on you between tries.
Stronger baby: lie flatter so lifting their head takes more work.
stopCues: Getting drowsy—move them to their back in their own sleep space

safety.text: Only while you're awake and alert. If you feel sleepy, put your baby on their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Lifting their head to see your face is tummy time: it builds the neck and shoulder strength babies use for rolling and sitting.

activities.title: Lap tummy time
activities.summary: Lay your baby tummy-down along your lap, support their head, and gently sway your knees while you talk.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

supervision.space: Seated securely with both feet down, one hand always on your baby.

steps: Sit with your knees together and lay your baby tummy-down along your thighs.
Keep their head in line with their body, supporting it with your hand as needed.
Stroke their back, talk softly, or sway your knees slowly from side to side.
adaptations: Turn them so they can see a window, a face, or a high-contrast picture.
Calmer baby: slow, rhythmic back pats; alert baby: chat and pause for their sounds.

safety.text: Keep a hand on your baby. If they fall asleep, move them onto their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Lap time is one of the tummy-time positions suggested for young babies who are still getting used to being on their tummy.

activities.title: Face-to-face floor tummy time
activities.summary: Put your baby tummy-down on a firm, flat mat on the floor and lie down at their eye level to chat.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

items: Firm play mat or a blanket on a clean floor

supervision.space: Firm, flat floor surface—never a bed, sofa, or cushion. Smooth the blanket so it can't bunch.

steps: Lay a firm mat or smoothed blanket on a clear patch of floor.
Place your baby tummy-down with their elbows tucked under their shoulders.
Lie down face to face and talk, sing, or hold a toy at their eye level.
Roll them onto their back for a rest when they've had enough.
adaptations: Short and often beats long: 1–3 minutes a few times a day is a fine start.
Add a high-contrast card or your face just in front to give them something to lift up for.

safety.text: Only while awake, with you right there. If they get sleepy, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Use the floor, not a bed or sofa.

why.text: Short, frequent tummy sessions on the floor help babies build the strength they'll use to roll, sit, and crawl.

activities.title: Tummy time reach and play
activities.summary: On a firm floor mat, place a toy just ahead or to one side so your baby lifts up, turns, and reaches.

notes: Your baby sets the pace; short, happy sessions count. Ask their clinician if they were born early.

items: 1–3 baby-safe toys or an unbreakable mirror

supervision.space: Firm, flat floor surface with a clear area around the mat; stay within arm's reach.

steps: Lay your baby tummy-down on a firm, flat mat on the floor.
Hold a toy or unbreakable mirror just in front, then move it slowly side to side.
Set it down a little to one side so they shift onto one arm to reach.
Let them get it before they get frustrated, then cheer their effort.
adaptations: Just starting out: keep the toy close and at eye level.
Pushing up on straight arms: place toys in a loose circle so they pivot to reach.

safety.text: Only while awake and watched. If they fall asleep, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Firm floor only; toys must be too big to fit in your baby's mouth.

why.text: Reaching for a toy on their tummy asks babies to lift, turn, and shift weight, building strength for rolling and crawling.

activities.title: Coo-and-copy chat
activities.summary: Hold your baby face to face, talk in a sing-song voice, then pause and copy any coo, smile, or face they make.

notes: Born early? Go by corrected age, and ask your baby's clinician about anything you're unsure of.

supervision.space: Anywhere you can sit and hold your baby with their face about 20–30 cm (8–12 in) from yours.

steps: Pick a calm, alert moment. Hold your baby so their face is about 20–30 cm (8–12 in) from yours, head supported.
Talk slowly in a sing-song voice: hello, their name, what you can see.
Pause and wait. When they coo, wriggle, or move their mouth, copy it back and add a word or two.
Try a slow face—stick out your tongue or open your mouth wide—then wait to see if they copy.
adaptations: Newborn: expect watching more than cooing; a few seconds of eye contact is their turn.
Once cooing starts, leave longer pauses so they can answer you.
Lying down? Put your baby on their back on the floor beside you, faces level.
stopCues: Looks away, turns their head, or closes their eyes

safety.text: Support their head and neck while you hold them.

why.text: Back-and-forth 'conversations' help babies learn that talk takes turns, and quick, warm replies show them they matter to you.

activities.title: Diaper-change chat
activities.summary: Turn a diaper change into chat time: say what you're doing, add a short rhyme, and never step away from your baby.

items: Wipes, or cotton wool and water

supervision.space: A mat on the floor is safest. On a raised surface, keep a hand on your baby and everything within reach.

steps: Gather everything first—diaper, wipes, clean clothes—so you never need to step away.
Lay your baby on a mat on the floor, or keep one hand on them the whole time on a changing table.
Say what you're doing with the same simple words each time: 'Legs up… new diaper… all done!'
Add a short rhyme or song, then finish with a smile and a cuddle.
adaptations: Very tired? Just narrate; no rhyme needed.
Walk your fingers up their leg for 'Round and round the garden' as you finish.
Upset by changes? Keep it brief and talk softly; chat time can wait.
stopCues: Seems cold—finish up and dress them

safety.text: Never leave your baby on a changing table, bed, or sofa, even for a second. A mat on the floor removes the drop.
Keep diaper sacks and other thin plastic out of your baby's reach.

why.text: Hearing the same words with the same actions, again and again, is how babies start to link words with what happens.

activities.title: Sway and hum
activities.summary: Hold your baby close with their head supported and sway or rock slowly while you hum or sing, seated or standing.

notes: Crying that won't settle or seems unusual? Call your baby's clinician; there may be a medical reason.

supervision.space: A clear path to sway in, or a chair you can rock in while staying wide awake.

steps: Check the basics first: fed, clean diaper, not too hot or cold.
Hold your baby against your chest or shoulder, one hand behind their head and neck.
Sway side to side, or rock in a chair, slow and smooth, while you hum or sing softly.
If they drift off, lay them on their back in their own sleep space.
adaptations: Too tired to stand? Rock in a chair, but only while you're wide awake.
Alert and happy? Put on music and slow-dance gently with them up on your shoulder.
Running on empty? Hand over to another adult if you can, even for a few minutes.
stopCues: Asleep—move them to their back in their own sleep space

safety.text: Support head and neck; keep movements slow and smooth. Never shake a baby. If you're overwhelmed, lay them in their crib and step away.
Rocking in a chair or on a sofa? Stay wide awake. If you feel sleepy, put your baby on their back in their own sleep space.
Watch your step while carrying, and don't hold a hot drink at the same time.

why.text: Rocking, swaying, and singing are among the ways AAP suggests trying to soothe a fussy baby, and being held close helps babies feel safe.

activities.title: Read aloud—any book
activities.summary: Hold your baby close and read anything aloud—a board book, a recipe, your own novel—in a warm, lively voice.

supervision.space: A comfortable seat where you can hold your baby close and stay awake.

steps: Settle with your baby in your lap or the crook of your arm, head supported.
Read aloud whatever you have. Use an expressive voice and let your pitch rise and fall.
Pause now and then to look at them and answer any sound or wriggle.
Stop whenever they've had enough; finishing doesn't matter.
adaptations: Have a board book? Hold a bold picture 20–30 cm from their face and talk about it.
Lying down? Read with your baby on their back on the floor beside you.
Read in whichever language feels most natural to you.

safety.text: Read only while you're wide awake. If either of you gets sleepy, put your baby on their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Babies don't need to follow the words: AAP says hearing your voice and being held close is what they benefit from most.

activities.title: Bold picture gazing
activities.summary: Hold a bold black-and-white picture 20–30 cm from your baby's eyes, let them look, and talk about what they see.

notes: Born early? Go by corrected age, and ask your baby's clinician about anything you're unsure of.

items: White card and a thick black marker
Or a board book with bold pictures

supervision.space: Baby on their back on a floor mat or in your lap; you hold the picture.

steps: Draw thick black stripes, a bullseye, or a simple face on white card, or open a bold-picture board book.
With your baby on their back or in your lap, hold it about 20–30 cm (8–12 in) from their eyes.
Wait for their gaze to settle, then name it: 'Stripes! Big black stripes.'
When they look away, switch pictures, or swap the picture for your own face.
adaptations: Newborn: one simple picture at a time is plenty.
Nearer 3 months: try a picture with more detail or color, or move it slowly to one side.
stopCues: Turns away or closes their eyes

safety.text: Hold the picture yourself and put it away afterward; keep loose items out of the sleep space.

why.text: In the early weeks babies see most clearly at about 20–30 cm and tend to prefer high-contrast patterns and faces.

activities.title: Rattle look-and-listen
activities.summary: Shake a rattle softly to one side of your baby's head, see if they look for it, then move it slowly across for their eyes to follow.

notes: Born early? Go by corrected age, and ask your baby's clinician about anything you're unsure of.

items: Or a clean sock on your hand as a puppet

supervision.space: Baby on their back on a floor mat, or in your lap facing you; the rattle stays in your hand.

steps: Lay your baby on their back on a mat, or hold them in your lap facing you.
About 20–30 cm to one side of their head, shake the rattle gently and wait.
If they turn or go still to listen, smile and tell them: 'You found it!'
Hold it where they can see it, then move it slowly to the other side for their eyes to follow.
adaptations: Newborn: they may only go still or blink; that counts as noticing.
No rattle? Pull a clean sock over your hand and move it slowly while you sing.
Try the other side next time.
stopCues: Startles or cries at the sound
Looks away or closes their eyes

safety.text: Use a baby rattle that's in one piece with no loose parts, and keep the sound soft.

why.text: Young babies notice movement and begin to turn toward sounds, so a soft sound and a slow-moving toy give them something to find.

activities.title: Pat-a-cake and toe rhymes
activities.summary: Say a rhyme while you gently clap your baby's hands together or pat their feet in time to the words.

supervision.space: Baby on their back on a floor mat, or in your lap facing you with their head supported.

steps: Lay your baby on their back on a mat, or hold them in your lap facing you with their head supported.
Hold their hands and gently bring them together as you say 'Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake…'.
Switch to their feet: pat the soles softly, or walk your fingers up their leg for 'Round and round the garden'.
Keep it slow and light, and end with a smile and a pause.
adaptations: Newborn: keep touches tiny and the rhyme slow; saying it while stroking one foot is enough.
Use any rhyme or song you know, in any language.

safety.text: Keep every touch gentle and let arms and legs move only as far as they go easily. Support their head if they're in your lap.

why.text: Rhymes with gentle touch are one way paediatric groups suggest sharing language with newborns, who tune in to rhythm and sound long before words.

activities.title: Gentle hand-and-foot massage
activities.summary: When your baby is calm and alert, stroke their hands, feet, and legs with slow, gentle, steady touches, watching how they respond.

notes: Born early, unwell, or have skin concerns? Ask your baby's clinician before starting massage.

items: Towel or mat on the floor

supervision.space: Baby on their back on a towel on the floor in a warm room, with you sitting or kneeling beside them.

steps: Pick a calm, alert time, not right after a feed or when they're hungry or tired.
Lay your baby on their back. Hold one hand, rest your thumb in their palm, and stroke slowly along their fingers.
Hold a foot in both hands and stroke from heel to toes, then make slow strokes down each leg.
Watch their face. If they relax, keep going; if they squirm or fuss, stop and try another day.
adaptations: Not sure they like it? Rest your hand still on their leg first, then try one slow stroke.
After a bath, wrapped in a towel, add a few long strokes down their arms and legs.

safety.text: Use gentle, steady pressure, never rough or fast, and stop if your baby seems uncomfortable.

why.text: AAP-published authors describe steady, gentle touch as calming for many babies, and it helps you learn what your baby likes.

activities.title: Diaper-off kick time
activities.summary: Lay your baby on their back on a towel on the floor with the diaper off for a few minutes so they can kick freely.

notes: Born early or have medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about floor play positions.

supervision.space: On the floor in a warm room, away from drafts and pets, with nothing that could fall on them.

steps: Spread a towel, with something waterproof under it, on the floor in a warm room.
Lay your baby on their back and take the diaper off. A top can stay on.
Let them kick and stretch. Sit beside them and talk about their busy legs, or touch the soles of their feet.
Put a fresh diaper on after a few minutes, or sooner if they seem chilly or fussy.
adaptations: Tired? Lie down beside them and chat face to face.
Fussy without the diaper? Try again another day with it on and their legs bare.

safety.text: Floor only, never a bed, sofa, or changing table. If they get sleepy, diaper on and onto their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: HSE suggests diaper-free time so young babies can kick their legs freely and use their muscles.

activities.title: Play-gym gazing on the mat
activities.summary: Lay your awake baby on their back under a play gym on the floor, staying in view while you do a quiet task nearby.

notes: Born early or have medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about floor play positions.

items: Baby play gym or floor-standing mobile

supervision.space: Clear floor you can see from your task. Nothing soft near their face; pets and older kids kept off the mat.

steps: Set the play gym over a firm mat on the floor where you can see it from your task.
Lay your baby on their back underneath, with toys high enough to look at but not tangle in.
Fold laundry or sit nearby, chatting and naming what they look at.
Look over often. Pick them up when they fuss, tire, or get drowsy.
adaptations: Newborn: one or two high-contrast toys are plenty.
Nearer 3 months: lower one toy to where their hands might swipe it.
No play gym? Lay them where they can watch you, a plant, or a window.

safety.text: Awake play only. If they get drowsy, move them onto their back in their own sleep space rather than leaving them on the mat.
Keep pillows, loose blankets, and soft toys away from their face. Use a sturdy gym with no long strings or cords.
Hang mobiles and toys only over the floor mat during awake play, never over the crib or bassinet.
If you’re cooking, set this up outside the cooking area and out of your path with hot pans.

why.text: Play on their back gives babies room to stretch and look around, and hanging toys give them something to watch and, later, swipe at.

activities.title: Side-lying play
activities.summary: Lay your awake baby on their side on a floor blanket, a rolled towel behind their back, and play with a toy or book in front.

notes: Head-shape, neck, or reflux concerns, or born early? Ask your baby's clinician which positions to use.

items: Blanket or mat on the floor

supervision.space: Firm floor surface, never a bed or sofa. Towel roll behind the back only, well away from their face.

steps: Lay a blanket flat on the floor and settle your baby on their side, a rolled towel behind their back if they tip.
Bring both arms forward and bend their knees a little so they're comfortable.
Hold a toy or book in front of them and chat; after a few minutes, switch to the other side.
Roll them onto their back to finish.
adaptations: Not enjoying tummy time yet? Side-lying is a gentler way to change position.
Lie down facing them so your face is the toy.
stopCues: Fussing or straining to roll back

safety.text: Awake play only: the side is not a safe sleep position. If they doze, move them onto their back in their own sleep space.
Floor only, and keep the towel roll behind their back, never near their face.

why.text: AAP suggests supported side-lying as another position for awake play, especially for babies who don't yet enjoy their tummy.

activities.title: Mirror hello
activities.summary: Hold your baby facing a mirror with you, point to both faces, and chat about the baby in the mirror.

items: A wall or wardrobe mirror, or a baby-safe mirror

supervision.space: Stand or sit in front of a mirror holding your baby, their head and neck supported.

steps: Hold your baby upright against your chest, or in your lap, facing a mirror, head supported.
Lean in close so both faces show. Smile and say, 'Who's that? That's you!'
Point to their nose, then yours. Pause and let them look.
Turn them back toward you when they've had enough.
adaptations: Newborn: get close to the mirror; faces far away are a blur.
Floor version: lay a baby-safe mirror beside them during floor play.

safety.text: Support their head and neck while you hold them.
Use a mirror fixed to the wall or furniture, or a shatterproof baby mirror, not a loose glass one.

why.text: Young babies are drawn to faces; a mirror gives them two to look at while you chat.

activities.title: Stroller stroll, point and name
activities.summary: Walk with your baby in a shaded stroller or pram, stopping now and then to show and name what you see and hear.

items: Stroller or pram with a sun canopy
Light covering clothes and a brimmed hat

supervision.space: Sidewalks or paths, shade from the canopy or trees, and nothing draped over the stroller front.

steps: Buckle your baby in lying back, canopy up, in light clothes that cover their arms and legs.
Pick a route with sidewalks or paths, and shade if it's sunny.
Every so often, stop, lean in, and name what they might see or hear: 'A big tree. Hear the bus?'
Head home if they fuss, get too warm or cool, or when you're done; an hour at most.
adaptations: Very tired? A slow loop of the block or the yard counts.
Fussy? Keep moving at a steady pace and talk or hum softly as you walk.
stopCues: Fussing that doesn't settle with a stop and a chat
Sweaty, flushed, or hot to touch
Cool hands and face, or shivering

safety.text: Under 6 months: AAP (2026) says keep babies out of direct and indirect sun (heat-stroke risk). Full shade, light long sleeves, a hat; not outside 10 a.m.–4 p.m.
Never drape a blanket over the stroller front; it traps heat and hides your baby. Buckle the harness every time.
Use sidewalks and crosswalks, watch for cars backing out of driveways, and keep your phone away when crossing.
If your baby falls asleep, move them onto their back on a firm, flat sleep surface as soon as you can.

why.text: A walk is one of the ways AAP suggests easing a fussy spell, and new sights and sounds give you plenty to name together.

activities.title: Home tour in your arms
activities.summary: Carry your baby slowly from room to room, in your arms or a carrier, stopping to show and name things: a window, a plant, a picture.

notes: Born early or breathing problems? AAP advises against upright carriers; ask your baby’s clinician about holding positions.

supervision.space: Clear walkways and stairs. Skip the stove and hot drinks while you're carrying your baby.

steps: Hold your baby upright on your shoulder or cradled in your arms, head supported, or use a carrier.
Walk slowly and stop at something interesting: a window, a plant, a picture, the mirror.
Bring them close and name it simply: 'Plant. Green leaves.' Watch their face.
If something catches their eye, stay a bit longer and talk about it.
adaptations: Fussy? Keep moving slowly and hum as you go.
Doing a small chore? Narrate it: 'Now we put the socks away.'

safety.text: Carrier: upright and snug, face visible, chin off chest, nose and mouth clear; check often. Under 4 months or born early? Take extra care.
Watch your step, use the handrail on stairs, and skip the stove and hot drinks while carrying.
If they fall asleep in your arms or the carrier, move them onto their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Naming what your baby is looking at, in short, simple words, is how early 'conversations' begin.

activities.title: Sit outside in the shade
activities.summary: Sit somewhere shady outdoors with your baby in your arms, and listen and look together: leaves, birds, a breeze.

items: Light covering clothes and a brimmed hat

supervision.space: Full shade on a porch, balcony, or under a tree, away from midday sun, in a seat where you stay alert.

steps: Dress your baby in light layers that cover their arms and legs, plus a brimmed hat if it's bright.
Find full shade and sit comfortably with them in your arms, head supported.
Notice things out loud together: 'Hear the bird? The leaves are moving.'
Go in if they get too warm or cool, or start to fuss.
adaptations: Fussy spell? A change of scene can help; keep your voice low and slow.
Windy, wet, or cold? Sit by an open door or window instead.
stopCues: Sweaty, flushed, or hot to touch
Cool hands and face, or shivering

safety.text: Under 6 months: AAP (2026) says keep babies out of direct and indirect sun (heat-stroke risk). Full shade, light long sleeves, a hat; not outside 10 a.m.–4 p.m.
Stay alert. If you feel yourself dozing, go in and put your baby on their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Outdoor sights and sounds give you lots to name together, and AAP notes a change of scene outside can help distract a fussy baby.

activities.title: Play-gym batting on the mat
activities.summary: Lay your baby on their back under a floor play gym so they can swipe, bat, and grab at the hanging toys while you stay nearby.

notes: Take the hanging toys down once your baby starts pushing up on hands and knees.
Born early? Use corrected age as a guide and ask your baby's clinician.

items: Floor play gym with toys on short, firm links
Firm play mat or blanket on the floor

supervision.space: Firm floor mat in your line of sight, away from sofa edges, pets, and older kids' small toys; look over often.

steps: Set the play gym over a firm mat on the floor, somewhere you can see your baby from your task.
Check each hanging toy is on a short, firm link and too big to fit in your baby's mouth.
Lay your baby on their back under the arch and move one toy so it catches their eye.
Glance over often and chat from where you are; swap a toy if they lose interest.
adaptations: Just starting to swipe: hang one toy low over their chest, close to their hands.
Grabbing well: move a toy down by their feet so they kick at it, or hang two toys to choose between.
stopCues: Fussing, crying, or turning away from the toys
Rubbing eyes, yawning, or going quiet and drowsy
Rolled onto their tummy and getting tired

safety.text: Hanging toys need short, secure links with no long strings. Take them down once your baby pushes up on hands and knees.
Your baby will mouth whatever they grab, so every toy must be clean and too big to fit in their mouth.
If they roll onto their tummy, come close and watch. If they get drowsy, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
If you’re cooking, set this up outside the cooking area and out of your path with hot pans.

why.text: Around 4 months many babies start swinging their arms at toys and holding what they touch; hanging toys give them something to aim for.

activities.title: Toe-catching on the mat
activities.summary: Lay your baby on their back on a floor mat with bare feet so they can kick, catch their knees and toes, and pull them to their mouth.

notes: Born early? Use corrected age as a guide and ask your baby's clinician.

items: Firm play mat or blanket on the floor

supervision.space: Firm floor mat in your line of sight, away from sofa edges, pets, and older kids' small toys; look over often.

steps: Check the room is comfortably warm, then lay a towel flat over a firm mat on the floor.
Lay your baby on their back with legs and feet bare; a loosened diaper, or none, gives more freedom.
Let them kick and stretch. Many babies this age start catching their knees and toes and pulling them to their mouth.
Look over and chat from nearby; a smile or a word back keeps them going.
adaptations: Not finding their feet yet? Kneel beside them, wiggle each toe through 'This Little Piggy', then lift their feet within reach of their hands.
Kicking a lot: hold a crinkly cloth book or soft toy by their feet so each kick makes it move.
stopCues: Getting cold: mottled skin or a cool tummy
Yawning, staring off, or getting drowsy

safety.text: Keep the towel flat under their hips with nothing soft by their face. If they get drowsy, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Floor only, never a bed or sofa: a kicking baby can scoot or roll off a raised surface.
If you’re cooking, set this up outside the cooking area and out of your path with hot pans.

why.text: Kicking freely on their back is a simple way to move, and between 4 and 7 months many babies discover they can catch their own feet.

activities.title: Chore chat from the play mat
activities.summary: Lay your baby on their back on a floor mat where they can see you, then talk them through a calm chore like folding laundry.

items: Firm play mat or blanket on the floor
A calm chore: laundry to fold, mail to sort

supervision.space: Mat in your line of sight, a little apart from your task; no cooking, hot drinks, or cords near the baby.

steps: Lay your baby on their back on a firm mat where they can see you, a little away from your work.
Talk about what you're doing as you go: 'One sock, two socks… here's a big blue towel.'
When they coo or kick, stop and answer them, then carry on.
Now and then hold something up to show them, like a bright T-shirt.
adaptations: Low on words today: hum or sing what you're doing instead of talking.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Rubbing eyes, yawning, or getting drowsy
Rolled onto their tummy and getting tired

safety.text: Keep laundry piles, bags, and cords off the mat and away from your baby's face.
Not while cooking or carrying hot drinks. If your baby gets drowsy, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
If you’re cooking, set this up outside the cooking area and out of your path with hot pans.

why.text: Hearing you talk about everyday things gives your baby lots of language to listen to, long before they understand the words.

activities.title: Follow and grab the rattle
activities.summary: Move a rattle slowly across your baby's view so they follow it, then hold it within reach so they can swipe, grab, shake, and mouth it.

notes: Born early? Use corrected age as a guide and ask your baby's clinician.

items: A light, easy-to-hold rattle too big to fit in the mouth
Optional second rattle or soft toy

supervision.space: Baby on a floor mat or supported in your lap, within arm's reach; not on a bed or other raised surface.

steps: With your baby on their back on the floor, hold a rattle about a forearm's length above their face.
Give it a soft rattle, then move it slowly side to side and up and down so their eyes can follow.
Bring it near their hands and let them swipe and grab; if they're new to it, place it in their palm.
Let them hold, shake, and mouth it. Once they've got it, offer a second toy to the other hand.
adaptations: Just starting: move it very slowly and keep it close; your face beside the rattle helps them find it.
Grabbing easily: hold it a little out of reach to one side so they stretch for it.
stopCues: Looking away or closing their eyes
Frustration when the toy stays out of reach

safety.text: Mouthing is expected: use a clean rattle that's too big to fit in their mouth, with no loose or small parts.
Choose a light rattle; babies this age often bop themselves while waving it.

why.text: Following a moving toy and then reaching for it links looking with hand movement; many babies around 4 months hold a toy placed in their hand.

activities.title: Babble copycat chat
activities.summary: Face to face, wait for your baby to coo or babble, copy the sound back, then pause so they can take another turn.

supervision.space: Anywhere you can be face to face and close: baby on a floor mat, in your lap, or buckled in a stroller.

steps: Get face to face, close enough that your baby can see your mouth, and wait quietly.
When they coo or babble, copy the sound back with a big, happy face.
Pause and wait; give them time to answer before you take your next turn.
If they repeat a sound like 'bah', say a few simple words that start with it.
adaptations: Quiet baby: start by copying their smiles, sighs, or tongue pokes, then add sounds.
Chattier baby: try a new sound, like a raspberry or 'ma', and see if they copy you.

safety.text: If they're in your arms, keep their head and neck supported. If they get drowsy, put them on their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Around 4 months many babies start to babble; copying them and waiting for a reply follows the turn-taking pattern of a conversation.

activities.title: Body-part action song
activities.summary: Sing 'Head, shoulders, knees and toes' slowly, gently touching each part or guiding your baby's hands to it as you name it.

supervision.space: Baby on a floor mat or supported in your lap facing you; not on a bed or other raised surface.

steps: Lay your baby on their back on a mat, or sit them supported in your lap facing you.
Sing slowly, touching each body part as you name it, or gently guiding their hands to it.
Pause before the last word and watch for a smile or kick, then finish with a cuddle or gentle tickle.
Sing it again a few times; babies enjoy the familiar pattern.
adaptations: Tired or fussy baby: sing softly and just hold their hands, without the actions.
Wants more: try 'Row, row, row your boat' with them supported in your lap, swaying slowly together.
stopCues: Pulling their hands away or stiffening

safety.text: Move their arms only as far as they go easily, and never pull or yank on a hand or arm.

why.text: Babies enjoy hearing the same rhymes again and again; that repetition, with your face, voice, and touch, is how they get to know sounds and words.

activities.title: Bold-picture book in your lap
activities.summary: Hold your baby in your lap and share a board or cloth book with bold pictures, pointing, using fun voices, and letting them touch and taste it.

items: 1–2 board, cloth, or vinyl books with bold, simple pictures

supervision.space: Seated somewhere comfortable with your baby in your lap and one arm around them; stay wide awake.

steps: Sit with your baby held securely in your lap and the book about a forearm's length from their face.
Point to one picture at a time and name it with lots of expression and different voices.
Let them pat, grab, and mouth the book; you don't need to finish it or read every word.
Close the book when they look away or fuss, and try again another time.
adaptations: Head control still developing: recline them against your chest so their head is supported.
Grabby baby: give them a cloth book to hold while you point at the pictures in yours.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.

safety.text: Use board, cloth, or vinyl books with no loose flaps, pieces, or ribbons, since the book will end up in their mouth.
Keep an arm around your baby and support their head while they're still steadying it.

why.text: Sharing books in the early months lets babies hear the rhythm and sounds of speech, and at 3–6 months a sturdy book is also something to reach for.

activities.title: Mirror faces together
activities.summary: Lie or sit with your baby in front of an unbreakable baby mirror, smile and make faces, and name their eyes, nose, and mouth.

supervision.space: Firm floor mat or your lap, within arm's reach; mirror set so it can't tip onto your baby.

steps: Prop an unbreakable baby mirror beside your baby on the floor mat, or hold it in front of them in your lap.
Put your face in the mirror next to theirs, then smile, raise your eyebrows, or stick out your tongue.
Touch and name their nose, eyes, and mouth, then point to the same parts in the mirror.
Pause and watch; if they smile, coo, or reach for the mirror, answer them.
adaptations: Younger or tiring easily: hold them reclined in your lap with the mirror close.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.

safety.text: Use only a baby mirror made of unbreakable plastic or mylar, never glass, and check it can't tip onto your baby.
Your baby will mouth the mirror: keep it clean and free of detachable parts.

why.text: Babies this age are drawn to faces, and many enjoy watching the baby in the mirror, especially closer to 6 months.

activities.title: Peekaboo with your hands
activities.summary: Face to face with your baby, cover your eyes with your hands, then uncover them with a happy 'peekaboo!' and watch how they react.

supervision.space: Anywhere your baby is safely settled and can see your face: floor mat, lap, or buckled in a stroller.

steps: Settle your baby where they can see your face up close, on a mat or in your lap.
Cover your eyes with your hands, wait a moment, then uncover them and say 'peekaboo!' with a big smile.
Wait for a smile, kick, or squeal before the next round; go slower if they startle.
adaptations: Younger or sensitive baby: keep it soft and slow, and don't stay hidden for long.
Ready for more: peek out from either side of a cloth you hold in front of your own face.

safety.text: Hide your own face, not your baby's, and keep any cloth away from their face.

why.text: Simple social games like peekaboo are suggested from around 4 months as a way to share attention and enjoy each other.

activities.title: Propped tummy time over a towel roll
activities.summary: On a firm floor mat, lay your baby tummy-down with a small rolled towel under their chest and arms, then play face to face.

notes: For babies who find flat tummy time hard. It is propped, so it doesn't count toward a flat-surface target.
Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

items: Firm play mat or blanket on the floor
Small hand towel rolled into a firm tube
A toy or unbreakable baby mirror

supervision.space: Firm floor surface, never a bed or sofa. Stay within arm's reach with eyes on your baby the whole time.

steps: Roll a small hand towel into a firm tube and lay it across a firm mat on the floor.
Place your baby tummy-down with the roll under their chest and armpits, arms forward over it.
Get down face to face, or set a toy just in front, so they lift and turn their head.
When they tire, take the roll away and let them rest on their back.
adaptations: Getting stronger: use a thinner roll, then none, moving toward flat tummy time on the mat.
Likes company: lie down facing them and chat while they work.
stopCues: Face dropping toward the towel or mat

safety.text: Awake and watched the whole time. If your baby gets drowsy, take the roll away and move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Keep the roll under the chest, never the face, and use it only on the floor, never on a bed or sofa.

why.text: A little lift under the chest can make it easier to raise the head on the tummy, which builds neck and shoulder strength.

activities.title: Tummy-to-back roll practice
activities.summary: During floor tummy time, move a toy up and over one shoulder so your baby turns to follow it and tips onto their back, with a gentle assist.

notes: Best once your baby can push up on their forearms during tummy time.
Born early or medical needs? Go by corrected age and ask your baby's clinician first.

items: Firm play mat or blanket on the floor

supervision.space: Firm floor with clear space on both sides; nothing hard, sharp, or small within rolling distance.

steps: Lay your baby tummy-down on a firm floor mat, up on their forearms if they can.
Show a toy in front, then move it slowly up and over one shoulder so they turn their head to follow.
As their weight shifts, you can gently guide their hip over so they tip onto their back.
Cheer when they land, and try the other side another time.
adaptations: Just starting: let them turn their head and shift weight to one side; finishing the roll can wait.
Rolling on their own: set the toy a little farther away so they roll and reach for it.
stopCues: Fussing, crying, or face dropping to the mat

safety.text: Tummy time only while awake and watched. If they get drowsy, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Guide the hip gently and let your baby lead the turn; never pull on an arm or the head.
Once your baby rolls, never leave them alone on a bed, sofa, or changing table, even for a moment.

why.text: Many babies roll tummy to back first, often between 3 and 6 months; a toy just out of reach gives them a reason to turn and roll.

activities.title: Side-lying two-hand play
activities.summary: Lay your baby on their side on a floor mat, a rolled towel behind their back, with a toy in front for both hands to reach; then switch sides.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician which play positions suit them.

items: Firm play mat or blanket on the floor
Hand towel rolled into a firm tube
A rattle, soft toy, or board book

supervision.space: Firm floor mat only. Stay within arm's reach; the towel stays behind the back, away from the face.

steps: Lay your baby on their side on a firm floor mat with a rolled towel snug behind their back.
Bring both arms forward and bend their hips and knees a little so they're comfy and steady.
Set a toy or book in front of their hands, close enough to touch, and chat to them.
After a few minutes, switch them to the other side or onto their back.
adaptations: Prefers one side: start on the side they like, then give the other side a shorter turn.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Rolling forward onto their face and fussing

safety.text: The towel roll is for awake, watched play only. If your baby gets drowsy, remove it and lay them on their back in their own sleep space.
Keep the towel behind their back, away from their face; if they roll forward onto it, lift it away.
Toys must be clean and too big to fit in their mouth.

why.text: Side-lying gives babies a different view and brings both arms forward to play; it's described as an alternative for babies who dislike tummy time.

activities.title: Supported sitting in your lap
activities.summary: Sit on the floor with your baby upright between your legs or in your lap, your hands low on their trunk, and a toy in front to look at and reach for.

notes: Best once your baby holds their head steady and lifts their chest during tummy time.
Born early? Go by corrected age and ask your baby's clinician.

items: A toy or board book to set in front

supervision.space: Sit on the floor, not a bed or sofa, with your baby between your legs or in your lap; hands on them throughout.

steps: Sit on the floor and settle your baby upright between your legs or in your lap, facing out.
Hold them around the hips or lower trunk, as low as still keeps them steady.
Put a toy in front at their eye level and let them lean, look, and reach for it.
When they slump or tire, lay them on the floor on their back or tummy for a change.
adaptations: Wobbly: hold higher, around the chest, and let them lean back against you.
Steadier: move your hands lower, or let them prop forward on their hands with a toy between them.
stopCues: Slumping, head bobbing, or leaning hard to one side

safety.text: Do this on the floor with your hands on your baby. Never leave a baby sitting on a raised surface, even for a moment.
Short, hands-on sitting practice is preferred over long stretches in seats or devices that prop a baby upright.

why.text: Once babies can lift their chest, holding them upright with something interesting in front lets them practice balancing and looking around.

activities.title: Texture touch tour
activities.summary: Brush a few clean, safe fabrics over your baby's hands and bare feet, naming each one: soft, bumpy, smooth, fuzzy.

items: Washcloth, cotton T-shirt, knit hat, or fleece

supervision.space: Baby on a firm floor mat or in your lap. You hold each fabric and take it away when done.

steps: Gather 3–4 clean fabrics that feel different, with no buttons, strings, or loose threads.
With your baby on their back or in your lap, brush one fabric over their palms and the soles of their feet.
Name it as they feel it, 'soft fleece', 'bumpy towel', and let them grab and mouth it while you hold the other end.
Take each one away before the next, and put them all out of reach when you finish.
adaptations: Easily overwhelmed: one fabric at a time, slowly, on the hands only.
Loves it: add a textured cloth book and talk about how each page feels.

safety.text: Anything they mouth must be clean, with no buttons, strings, or loose threads that could come off.
Keep hold of each fabric yourself and keep cloth away from your baby's face; clear everything away when you finish.
If your baby gets drowsy, clear the fabrics and lay them on their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Feeling different textures with their skin, hands, and mouth is one of the ways babies explore, and naming them adds words to the experience.

activities.title: Sleeve peekaboo while dressing
activities.summary: While dressing your baby, say each step in the same few words and play 'Where's your hand? There it is!' as each hand comes through a sleeve.

items: The next outfit, laid out within reach

supervision.space: Changing mat on the floor is safest. On any raised surface, keep one hand on your baby the whole time.

steps: Lay your baby on their back on a changing mat on the floor, with the next outfit within reach.
Say each step in the same short words every time: 'Arm in… head through… socks on!'
Gather a sleeve, reach in from the cuff to hold their hand, and ease it through: 'Where's your hand? There it is!'
Pause for their smile or coo, answer them, then do the next sleeve or sock.
adaptations: Fussy about dressing: keep it short and sing one familiar line instead of the game.
Enjoying it: hide and find their feet in the legs of a sleepsuit the same way.
stopCues: Crying or stiffening: finish quickly and calmly

safety.text: Never leave your baby alone on a changing table, bed, or other raised surface, even for a few seconds.
Ease clothes on without pulling, twisting, or over-stretching arms and legs, and support their head as tops go over it.
Skip clothes with drawstrings and hats with cords or ties.

why.text: Dressing is face-to-face time; using the same words for each step, plus a little game, gives your baby repeated language to tune into.

activities.title: Shaded stroller or carrier walk
activities.summary: Take a short walk with your baby fully shaded in a stroller with the canopy up, or in a carrier, and name what you see along the way.

notes: Born early or breathing problems? AAP advises against upright carriers; ask your baby’s clinician about holding positions.

items: Stroller with a sunshade canopy, or a baby carrier
Light long sleeves, long pants, and a wide-brimmed hat

supervision.space: Sidewalks or park paths with baby fully shaded; on sunny days go before 10 a.m. or after 4 p.m.; skip it in heat.

steps: Pick a cooler time (before 10 a.m. or after 4 p.m. on sunny days) and dress your baby in light clothes that cover arms and legs, plus a hat.
Put the stroller canopy up so they stay in shade, or use a carrier with their face visible and chin off their chest.
Stop now and then to point at and name what they're looking at: a tree, a dog, a bus.
Head home well within an hour, or sooner if they fuss or seem too warm.
adaptations: Hot or glaring day: walk somewhere fully shaded or indoors instead, or skip it.
Fussy in the stroller: try a carrier so they're close to you, keeping their face visible.
Two children? Use a together walk idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Flushed, sweaty, or unusually fussy (too warm)

safety.text: Under 6 months: AAP (2026) says keep babies out of direct and indirect sun (heat-stroke risk). Full shade, light long sleeves, a hat; not outside 10 a.m.–4 p.m.
In a carrier, keep their face visible, chin off their chest, and nose and mouth clear, and check on them often.
If your baby falls asleep in the stroller or carrier, move them to their back on a firm, flat sleep surface as soon as you can.
Stick to sidewalks and paths, and set the stroller brake whenever you stop.

why.text: A walk shows your baby new sights and sounds, and pointing out and naming what they notice turns it into a conversation.

activities.title: Peekaboo with a cloth
activities.summary: Drape a light cloth over your own head, wait for your baby to pull it off, then greet them with a happy “Peekaboo!”

items: Your hands, or a light cloth or dish towel

supervision.space: Baby on the floor, in a seat, or on your lap, face to face. The cloth stays in your hands, never over your baby's face.

steps: Sit face to face with your baby, close enough to touch.
Drape a light cloth over your head and ask, “Where did I go?”
Wait for your baby to pull it off—or lift it yourself after a second or two—and greet them with a big “Peekaboo!”
Take turns: hide behind your hands, a cushion, or the cloth again.
adaptations: Just starting: keep hides very short and your voice soft so a disappearing face isn't startling.
Older baby: hide a toy under the cloth while they watch, then let them lift it to find the toy.
On the move: peek out from behind a doorway or the sofa and let them come and find you.
stopCues: Startled crying when your face disappears

safety.text: Put the cloth over your own head or the toy, never your baby's face, and put it away when the game ends.

why.text: Watching a face or toy disappear and come back plays into babies' growing understanding that things still exist when they can't see them.

activities.title: Put in, tip out
activities.summary: Sit with your baby and take turns dropping big blocks or cups into a bowl, then tip them all out and start again.

items: Plastic cups, big lids, or balled-up socks
Large blocks or stacking cups, if you have them

supervision.space: Clear floor with your baby sitting steadily; nothing small enough to fit through a toilet-paper tube within reach.

steps: Gather a big bowl or box and a handful of large, unbreakable things.
Drop one in with a clear “in!” and hand your baby the next one.
When the bowl is full, tip it out together—“all out!”—and start again.
Follow your baby's lead; banging or mouthing the cups is part of the game.
adaptations: Simpler: you fill the bowl and let your baby do the tipping out.
Harder: cut a wide slot in a box lid for posting large jar lids or balled-up socks (each too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube) or balled-up socks.
Hide a toy inside a cup or box for them to find.
stopCues: Frustration when things won't go in

safety.text: Use only items too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube, with no loose bits that could break off.

why.text: Filling and emptying lets babies explore how objects fit inside one another—one of the ways they work out shapes and sizes.

activities.title: Pots and wooden spoon band
activities.summary: Set a couple of cold pots and a wooden spoon on the floor and make some noise together—tap, bang, and copy each other.

items: Two or three cold pots or pans
Plastic tubs or a silicone spatula (quieter)

supervision.space: Floor well away from the stove, hot drinks, and kettle cords—a time when you're not cooking.

steps: Turn two or three cold pots upside down on the floor and add a wooden spoon.
Tap a pot and say “bang!”, then hand your baby the spoon.
Copy whatever your baby does—loud, soft, fast, slow—and see if they copy you back.
adaptations: Quieter: swap metal pots for plastic tubs and a silicone spatula.
Older baby: sing a simple song and tap along to the beat together.
Sound-sensitive baby: start with one soft tap and watch their face before going louder.
stopCues: Startling or crying at loud bangs

safety.text: Never while you're cooking: keep the band away from the stove and hot drinks, and don't hold your baby near hot pans.
Check every item passes the toilet-paper-tube test and has no knobs or parts that come off.

why.text: Many babies around this age love banging things together and discovering that they're the ones making the sound.

activities.title: Treasure basket of household things
activities.summary: Fill a low basket with a few sturdy household things of different textures and sounds, and sit close while your baby explores.

notes: Everything will go in the mouth at this age, so choose every item with that in mind.

items: A low, sturdy basket or box
Saucepan lid without a removable knob

supervision.space: Floor, baby sitting steadily, you within arm's reach and watching. Household items aren't safety-tested toys.

steps: Pick 5–8 sturdy household things with different textures, weights, and sounds.
Check each one: too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube, nothing loose or breakable, clean enough to mouth.
Sit your baby beside the basket and let them choose. Stay close and quiet, smiling or naming things when they look up.
Another day, swap in a couple of new items to keep it interesting.
adaptations: Less steady sitter: sit them in your lap and offer one item at a time.
Theme it: all wooden, all metal, or all soft things.
Older baby: add a second container so they can move things between the two.
stopCues: Gagging on an item—take it away

safety.text: Household things aren't safety-tested toys: stay with your baby the whole time and remove anything that cracks, splinters, or comes apart.
Every item must be too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube. Leave out keys, coins, batteries, small balls, and small lids.

why.text: Babies this age learn by handling and mouthing objects, noticing textures, weights, and sounds—a treasure basket offers lots of that in one place.

activities.title: Cushion hills crawl course
activities.summary: Lay sofa cushions and pillows flat on the floor as low hills, put a favourite toy on the far side, and cheer your baby over.

notes: Bottom-shuffling or tummy-creeping counts too—follow how your baby moves.

supervision.space: Clear floor away from stairs and hard furniture edges; cushions low and firm; you within arm's reach the whole time.

steps: Lay a few firm cushions or pillows flat on the floor to make low bumps.
Put a favourite toy on the far side and call your baby.
Stay alongside, cheer them over, and pop up from behind a cushion for a peekaboo.
Rearrange the hills once they've got the hang of it.
adaptations: Just starting to move: one flat cushion and a toy just out of reach is plenty.
Confident crawler: add a short, open-ended box tunnel you can see through, and wait at the exit.
Shufflers and scooters: make the course flatter and wider.

safety.text: Stay right there: a baby who slips between cushions or under a box may not be able to get out and could smother.
Build it on the floor only—never on a bed or sofa—and away from stairs (gate them) and hard furniture edges.

why.text: Low hills give babies a reason to move, and moving around—however they do it—is how they explore and build strength.

activities.title: Roll the ball back and forth
activities.summary: Sit facing your baby, legs spread to make a fence, and gently roll a big soft ball between you, taking turns.

supervision.space: Clear floor, or a blanket on flat grass in the shade; sit close enough that the ball comes straight back.

steps: Sit facing your baby, close together, with your legs out to stop the ball escaping.
Roll the ball slowly to them and say “your turn!”
Help them push it back, then cheer: “my turn!”
adaptations: Wobbly sitter: sit behind them and push the ball together toward a wall or another adult.
Crawler: roll the ball slowly past them and let them crawl after it.
Outdoors: play on a blanket on flat grass in the shade.
stopCues: Frustration when the ball rolls away

safety.text: Use a ball far too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube—small balls are a choking hazard.

why.text: Rolling a ball back and forth is turn-taking at its simplest, and it asks for balance and planning a movement.

activities.title: Cruise along the sofa
activities.summary: Line a few toys along a sturdy sofa so your baby can pull up and side-step from one to the next while you stay close.

items: A sturdy sofa or anchored low furniture

supervision.space: Stable sofa or anchored furniture with no sharp corners; clear floor; away from windows, stairs, and TV stands.

steps: Check the sofa is stable and clear hard toys and sharp-cornered furniture from the floor around it.
Set toys along the seat a short step apart, starting where your baby pulls up.
Stay alongside as they side-step to the next toy, and cheer each step.
If they get stuck standing, show them how to bend their knees and sit down.
adaptations: Just pulling up: one toy on the seat right above where they're kneeling.
Steadier: space toys a little farther apart, or around the corner of the sofa.
Pushing practice: a sturdy, weighted push toy or an empty cardboard box to push across the floor.

safety.text: Only use furniture that can't tip or slide. Anchor dressers, bookcases, and TV stands, and keep tempting things off high surfaces.
Skip the wheeled baby walker: walkers lead to falls, including down stairs. Gate the stairs and keep climbable furniture away from windows.

why.text: Pulling up and side-stepping along furniture is how many babies practise standing and stepping before walking on their own.

activities.title: Point-and-name book time
activities.summary: Cuddle up with a board or lift-the-flap book, point to the pictures, and name them—no need to read every word.

supervision.space: Your lap or a floor cushion, with your baby sitting supported against you.

steps: Sit your baby on your lap facing the book, or lie side by side on the floor.
Point to a picture and name it simply: “Dog! Woof woof.”
Pause to let them pat, lift flaps, or babble—then answer what they ‘said’.
Stop while it's still fun; a page or two counts.
adaptations: Younger: photo books of faces and familiar things.
Older: ask “Where's the ball?” and let them pat or point to it.
Outdoors: take the books onto a blanket in the shade.

safety.text: Chewing books is normal. Choose sturdy board or cloth books and remove any with loose flaps or peeling pieces.

why.text: Naming pictures and answering your baby's babble surrounds them with words and turn-taking, and sharing a book is good bonding time.

activities.title: Clapping and waving songs
activities.summary: Sing a simple action song—pat-a-cake, wave bye-bye, “if you're happy and you know it”—and do the moves with your baby.

supervision.space: Baby on your lap, strapped in a high chair, or sitting on the floor facing you.

steps: Sit face to face so your baby can see your hands and face.
Sing slowly with big, clear moves: clap, wave, pat your knees.
Gently clap their hands together, then pause to see if they try it themselves.
Repeat favourites—babies love knowing what comes next.
adaptations: Younger: sing and move your own hands; guide theirs only if they enjoy it.
Older: wait for them to start the clap or wave, then sing on cue.
Wave “hello” and “bye-bye” for real at people, pets, and the bath water draining.
stopCues: Looking away or going quiet and still

safety.text: Keep moves gentle: guide hands softly, support your baby's body, and never jerk or shake them.

why.text: Songs, clapping, and waving pair words with gestures, which helps babies follow what you mean and join in before they can talk.

activities.title: Name body parts while dressing
activities.summary: As you dress or change your baby on the floor, name each body part you touch—“arm in… there's your hand!”—and pause for a reaction.

items: A changing mat or towel on the floor

supervision.space: Changing mat or towel on the floor, with everything you need within reach before you start.

steps: Lay a mat or towel on the floor and put the clothes within reach.
Name each part as it goes in: “Arm in… hand out! Where's your foot?”
Tickle or kiss the part you named, then pause and let your baby react.
adaptations: Younger: just name and touch—“toes, toes, toes.”
Older: ask “Where's your tummy?” and let them pat it or point.
Add a body-part song, like “Head, shoulders, knees and toes.”
stopCues: Tired and wanting to be held

safety.text: Dress and change on the floor once your baby rolls. Never leave them on a changing table, bed, or sofa, even for a second.

why.text: Naming body parts during everyday care links words to things your baby can see and feel, over and over.

activities.title: Splash and pour water play
activities.summary: In a shallow bath or a basin of water, let your baby splash, pour from cups, and squeeze a sponge while you stay hand-close.

items: Bath or wide basin with a few centimetres of water
Plastic cups or a clean squeezy bottle

supervision.space: Bath, or a basin on the floor; shallow lukewarm water; towel and toys within reach so you never step away.

steps: Gather the towel, cups, and sponge first so you won’t need to leave.
Run a few centimetres of water, cold first, and check it with your wrist or elbow.
Kneel beside your baby with one hand on them the whole time (touch supervision); show pouring and squeezing with the other.
Lift them out onto the towel and empty the water straight away.
adaptations: Less steady sitter: support their back as well as keeping your hand on them.
Older baby: add a colander or a cup with holes and watch the water rain out.
Make it bath time: name each body part as you wash it.
stopCues: Fussing or trying to climb out

safety.text: Keep a hand on your baby every second. If the door or phone needs you, lift your baby out and take them with you.
A bath seat or ring is not a safety device—seats can tip and babies can slip out.
Test the water with your wrist or elbow first, and empty the bath or basin as soon as you finish.

why.text: Pouring, squeezing, and splashing let babies see how water and objects behave, and naming what happens adds words to the fun.

activities.title: Blanket on the grass
activities.summary: Spread a blanket on shady grass and let your baby feel the grass edge, a big leaf, and the breeze while you name what they touch.

items: Sun hat and light clothes that cover skin

supervision.space: Shady, flat grass in your yard or a nearby green space, away from traffic, water, and recently sprayed lawns.

steps: Check the patch for small stones, sticks, litter, droppings, or mushrooms, then spread the blanket in the shade.
Sit with your baby near the blanket's edge so they can reach out and pat the grass.
Offer a big leaf to crinkle and name things: “Grass—tickly!” “A bird—tweet!”
Wash hands when you head back inside.
adaptations: Crawler: let them crawl onto the grass while you stay alongside.
Add outdoor story time with a board book.
stopCues: Fussing, or seeming too hot or cold
Putting grass, soil, or leaves in their mouth again and again

safety.text: Use shade, a hat, and light clothes that cover skin, and avoid the strongest midday sun. From 6 months, sunscreen can go on exposed skin.
Clear away anything small enough to mouth, and skip lawns treated in the last 48 hours or spots with poisonous plants.

why.text: Grass, leaves, breezes, and birdsong give babies a rich mix of things to feel, hear, and see.

activities.title: Narrated stroller walk
activities.summary: Head out with the stroller or carrier and keep up a running commentary—stop to name the dog, bus, or tree your baby is watching.

items: Stroller with a five-point harness, or a baby carrier

supervision.space: Sidewalks and paths, kept back from the curb and traffic; harness on, brake set whenever you stop.

steps: Buckle the five-point harness and dress your baby for the weather.
As you walk, name what you see: “Dog! Big dog. Woof!”
Every few minutes, set the brake, crouch to your baby's level, and talk about whatever they're watching.
Answer their babbles as if it's a conversation.
adaptations: In a carrier: keep their face visible and chin off their chest.
Older baby: stop and ask “Where's the bus?” and wait for a look or a point.
Rainy day: do the same thing at a window or under a covered porch.
stopCues: Fussing or arching in the seat
Falling asleep—keep them in view, then move them to a firm, flat sleep space at home

safety.text: Use the five-point harness every ride, set the brake whenever you stop, keep bags off the handles, and stay with your baby.
In a carrier, keep your baby's face visible, chin off their chest, and nose and mouth clear.
If your baby falls asleep, move them onto their back on a firm, flat sleep surface as soon as you can.
In strong sun, use the canopy or shade, a hat, and light clothes that cover skin.

why.text: Talking about what your baby is looking at helps them link words to the things right in front of them.

activities.title: Bucket swing at the playground
activities.summary: Settle your baby in a full bucket-seat swing, stand in front, and give small, slow pushes while you chat and smile.

notes: Only in a full bucket seat that supports your baby on all sides and between the legs.

items: A playground with infant bucket-seat swings

supervision.space: Infant bucket swing over soft playground surfacing, not grass or concrete; you in front, clear of other swings.

steps: Check the seat is an intact full bucket swing over soft surfacing, and touch it for heat on sunny days.
Lift your baby in, legs through the leg holes, and check they're sitting upright.
Stand in front and give small, slow pushes; eye contact and a “wheee!” make it a game.
Lift them out yourself when they've had enough.
adaptations: First time: keep pushes tiny and stay face to face so they can see you.
Enjoying it: add “Ready, steady… go!” before each push.
Busy playground: wait for a quiet swing bay away from big kids' swings.
stopCues: Gripping tight, crying, or looking scared
Turning away or reaching to get out

safety.text: Stay at the swing with eyes on your baby, keep pushes low, and watch for children walking in front of swings.
Use only a full bucket seat made for babies and toddlers, and lift your baby in and out yourself.
Check seats and chains for heat in strong sun, and dress your baby for the weather.
Hold hands in the parking lot and near roads on the way there and back.

why.text: Gentle swinging is a sensory experience that many children find calming.

activities.title: Play yard play while you work nearby
activities.summary: Put your baby in a safe play yard with two or three toys where you can see them, and chat to them as you do a nearby task.

notes: Stop using the play yard once your baby can climb out or reaches about 35 in (89 cm) tall.

items: A play yard (playpen) in good repair
Two or three safe toys or board books

supervision.space: Play yard in your line of sight, well away from the stove, hot drinks, blind cords, and anything a standing baby could grab.

steps: Set up the play yard with every side fully up and locked, where you can see it from your task.
Add two or three safe toys or board books—nothing strung across the top and nothing to climb on.
Talk to your baby as you work: say what you're doing and answer their sounds.
Check on them often, and lift them out when they fuss or you're done.
adaptations: Cooking: keep the play yard well away from the stove and out of the path you walk with hot pans.
Fussy after a few minutes: swap one toy, or move the play yard closer to where you're working.
Older baby: rotate toys between sessions so there's something new each time.
stopCues: Crying or reaching to be picked up
Tired, rubbing eyes, or falling asleep

safety.text: Keep the sides fully up and the mesh intact. Remove hanging toys and changing-table add-ons, and anything a standing baby could climb on.
Never cook or carry hot drinks while holding or wearing your baby—that's what the play yard is for.
Place the play yard away from window-blind, curtain, and appliance cords.
If your baby falls asleep, lay them on their back in their own firm, flat sleep space with nothing else in it.

activities.title: Free explore in a baby-safe room
activities.summary: Let your crawler roam a baby-proofed, gated room with a few toys while you do a task in the same room and check in often.

items: Baby gate or a closed door
Furniture anchors and cupboard locks in place

supervision.space: Gated, baby-proofed room: anchored furniture; no cords, small objects, open stairs, or hot drinks; you stay in the room.

steps: Sweep the floor: check under furniture and between cushions for anything small.
Close the gate or door, and move cords, cleaning products, and hot drinks out of reach.
Scatter a few safe toys and let your baby choose where to go.
Do your task in the same room, glancing over often and chatting when they look up.
adaptations: Not crawling yet: use a play yard instead.
Starting to pull up: re-check that every piece of furniture in the room is stable or anchored.
Rotate a different basket of toys each day.
stopCues: Crying or wanting to be held
Heading again and again for something off-limits

safety.text: Before play, check under furniture and between cushions for coins, batteries, and other small things, and keep older children's toys out.
Anchor tip-prone furniture and TVs, gate the stairs, and keep climbable furniture away from windows.
Keep blind and appliance cords out of reach, and lock away medicines and cleaning products.
A safe room buys you time, not a break from watching: stay in the room and keep your baby in sight.

why.text: Moving around a safe space lets babies choose where to go and what to explore, building strength as they go.

activities.title: Push a box or push toy around
activities.summary: Let your toddler push an empty laundry basket, a big box or a sturdy push toy around a cleared, gated room while you stay in view.

notes: Not a walking timeline: some toddlers push before walking, others after.
Baby walkers aren't recommended; a box or push toy they steer themselves is different.

items: Empty laundry basket or sturdy cardboard box
A soft toy to give a ride

supervision.space: Cleared floor in the room you're in; stairs gated, sharp corners out of the way, heavy furniture anchored.

steps: Clear a path, check stairs are gated, and move anything sharp or breakable out of the way.
Hand over an empty laundry basket, big box or stable push toy, with a teddy inside for a ride.
Let them push it round the room while you stay in view; cheer when they turn a corner or bring teddy to you.
adaptations: Just pulling up: a heavier box that slides slowly gives steadier support than a toy on wheels.
Steady walker: make it a delivery game, pushing toys from one side of the room to the other.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Frustrated when the box keeps getting stuck
Falling a lot or getting tired
Climbing into or onto the box

safety.text: Gate stairs and keep the path clear of sharp furniture corners; toddlers fall often as they learn to walk.
Anchor dressers, shelves and TVs: toddlers who pull up and cruise use furniture to steady themselves.
If you’re cooking, set this up outside the cooking area and out of your path with hot pans.

why.text: CDC suggests letting toddlers push things like empty boxes, a child-size chair or push toys so they can practice walking.

activities.title: Kick and chase a big ball
activities.summary: Out in an open space, kick, roll or throw a big soft ball for your walking toddler to chase, then take turns sending it back.

items: Soft ball bigger than your toddler's fist

supervision.space: Open floor or grass away from stairs, breakables, roads and driveways.

steps: Pick a soft ball bigger than your toddler’s fist and find open floor or grass.
Roll or gently kick it a few steps ahead and let them walk or run after it.
Take turns sending it back: “My turn, your turn!” Try a kick or a two-handed throw.
adaptations: Wobbly walker: roll it slowly a short way ahead and let them walk after it.
Steady runner: kick it at a wall or into a laundry-basket “goal”.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Throwing the ball at faces or at a baby

safety.text: Use a soft ball too big to fit in the mouth; small balls are a choking hazard for under-3s.
Outdoors, use a fenced yard or enclosed play area well away from the street and driveways. An adult fetches anything that rolls toward a road.

why.text: AAP says toddlers learn how their bodies work by walking, running and kicking balls, and that playing together supports physical and social skills.

activities.title: Freeze dance
activities.summary: Put on music and dance together; when you pause it, everyone freezes, then dances again when it restarts.

notes: Younger toddlers may keep dancing through the pauses; that's fine.

items: Music on a phone or speaker (screen face down)

supervision.space: Clear floor away from stairs, sharp table corners and hard edges.

steps: Clear a little floor space and put on a song with a strong beat.
Dance together: stomp, wiggle, clap and copy each other's moves.
Pause the music and freeze like statues, then restart it and cheer the unfreeze.
Keep pauses short and silly so the stopping stays fun.
adaptations: Not walking yet: sway, clap and wave while sitting or holding the sofa.
Older toddler: freeze in a shape: tall, tiny or like an animal.
Winding down: slow songs and slow-motion moves.

safety.text: Dance on a clear floor away from stairs and sharp corners; socks can slip on smooth floors.

why.text: ZERO TO THREE describes freeze games as practice in listening and in stopping and starting; AAP suggests dancing together and copying moves.

activities.title: Bubble pop outside
activities.summary: Blow bubbles outdoors for your toddler to point at, chase and pop, saying 'pop!' each time.

items: Bubble solution and wand (you hold them)

supervision.space: Grass or a fenced yard or park, away from roads, ponds and paddling pools; the bottle stays with you.

steps: Head outside to grass or a fenced yard and keep the bubble bottle in your hand or pocket.
Blow a few bubbles and point: 'Look, bubbles!' Let your toddler reach, clap or stomp to pop them.
Pause between rounds so they can ask for 'more' with a word, a sign or a look.
adaptations: Not walking yet: sit them on the grass and blow bubbles low and slow.
Steady runner: blow a long stream and let them chase it across the grass.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Grabbing for the bottle to drink

safety.text: Keep the bottle with you and watch that your toddler doesn't eat bubbles or drink the solution.
Use shade, a hat and covering clothes, and sunscreen on exposed skin; avoid the midday sun.
Outdoors, use a fenced yard or enclosed play area well away from the street and driveways.

why.text: AAP suggests blowing bubbles for younger toddlers to point at and letting older ones chase and pop them; CDC treats bubble popping as a turn-taking game.

activities.title: Action songs with pauses
activities.summary: Sing an action song like “Wheels on the Bus” or a body-part song, and pause before an action or word so your toddler can fill it in.

supervision.space: Anywhere you can sit face to face, on the floor or a low seat.

steps: Sit face to face so your toddler can see your hands and mouth.
Sing a short song with big, simple actions: rolling hands, clapping, touching your nose.
Slow down and pause before an action or a last word so they can try it.
Repeat favorites; the same song many times over is normal.
adaptations: Younger toddler: gently help their hands do one action, then let them watch you.
Older toddler: let them pick the song and lead the actions.
Swap in body parts or family names to keep it fresh.

safety.text: If they're on your lap, sit on the floor or a low seat so a sudden wriggle isn't a fall.

why.text: CDC suggests songs with gestures and body-part songs where you pause for your toddler to join in, to help them learn body-part names.

activities.title: “Where’s the dog?” picture book
activities.summary: Share a board book, ask “Where’s the…?” questions your toddler answers by pointing, and add a few words to each picture they show you.

items: 2–3 board books with big, clear pictures

supervision.space: A quiet, comfortable spot with the TV off, on the floor or a low sofa.

steps: Find a quiet spot with the TV off and let your toddler choose a book.
Ask questions they can answer by pointing: “Where’s the ball? Where’s the cat’s nose?”
When they point, add a few words: “Yes, the dog. The dog says woof!”
Let them turn pages and skip around; you don’t need to finish the book.
adaptations: Just starting to point: you point and name, and let them copy the animal sounds.
Older toddler: pause before a familiar word in a favorite book and let them fill it in.
Low on energy: one favorite page, looked at a few times, is plenty.
stopCues: Chewing the pages more than looking

safety.text: Use board books and check for loose flaps, foam pieces or stickers that could come off in the mouth.

why.text: AAP says sharing books can help toddlers learn to talk, and suggests naming the pictures your child points to and asking questions they can answer by pointing.

activities.title: Busy basket in a gated play space
activities.summary: Before you cook or do a task, set out a basket of large, safe toys and board books in a gated, child-proofed spot you can see.

items: Small pot or plastic bowl and a wooden spoon

supervision.space: Gated, child-proofed spot outside the kitchen but in your view; nothing on shelves to climb for.

steps: Before the stove goes on, set up a playpen or gated play space outside the kitchen where you can see it.
Fill a basket with 5–8 large items: board books, big blocks, stacking cups, a soft toy, a pot and spoon.
Check the floor and under cushions for small things, then let them explore.
Glance over often and chat from where you are; swap in a 'new' item if they get bored.
adaptations: Younger toddler: fewer items, plus a box to put things in and take out.
Older toddler: add a 'job', like socks to sort or a dry cloth to wipe the toy table.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Crying at the gate or trying to climb it

safety.text: While you cook, keep your toddler out of the kitchen; a playpen or gated space you can see is safer than underfoot.
Only items too big to fit in the mouth; check under cushions and furniture for coins, batteries and small toys.
Anchor shelves and keep tempting things off high surfaces in that space.

activities.title: Stack it and knock it down
activities.summary: Build a tower of big blocks, empty boxes or plastic cups and let your toddler knock it down, then take turns building again.

supervision.space: Floor space well away from a baby's mat so falling blocks don't land on anyone.

steps: Gather big blocks, stacking cups or empty boxes, nothing small enough to fit in the mouth.
Stack three or four and invite your toddler to knock them down: 'Ready... crash!'
Take turns: they add one, you add one, then down it goes again.
adaptations: Younger toddler: you build, they topple, as many times as it's fun.
Older toddler: line boxes up as a train or build a wall to peek over.
Two children? Use a side-by-side or together idea for both ages instead.
stopCues: Upset every time a tower falls

safety.text: Use blocks and cups too big to fit in the mouth; pull staples, tabs and wrapping off boxes first.
Build away from a baby; toppling or thrown blocks can hit a little one.

why.text: CDC suggests playing with blocks and toys that get hands busy, from stacking for your toddler to knock down to taking turns building towers.

activities.title: Fill-and-dump basket relay
activities.summary: Show your toddler how to carry rolled socks or soft toys from one basket to another a few steps away, then dump and start again.

items: Two baskets, boxes or large pans
Rolled pairs of socks or soft toys

supervision.space: Clear floor in a gated, child-proofed room you're in; nothing small in the baskets.
